column1: What are the three core invariants of a well-designed ML pipeline?
column2: 1) Referential Transparency of Data (bit-for-bit reproducible artifacts), 2) Schema-Contract Enforcement at every stage boundary, 3) Separation of Code, Data, and Configuration.

column1: Why must schema contract violations cause hard failures rather than warnings in an ML pipeline?
column2: Because schema drift (silent upstream field changes) is the most common cause of silent model degradation in production; warnings allow corrupted data to silently propagate.

column1: What does feature engineering formally accomplish in terms of function approximation?
column2: It constructs a transformation φ: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ such that the composition f ∘ φ⁻¹ becomes learnable by the chosen hypothesis class (e.g., mapping XOR to a linearly separable space).

column1: What is the mutual information formula I(X;Y) and what does I(X;Y)=0 imply for a feature?
column2: I(X;Y) = Σ_{x,y} p(x,y) log[p(x,y)/(p(x)p(y))]. If I(X;Y)=0, the feature X is statistically independent of target Y, adding zero predictive signal while increasing VC dimension and loosening generalization bounds.

column1: What is the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle's implication for feature redundancy?
column2: The best model is the one that most compresses the data; thus the ideal feature set maximizes I(Xᵢ;Y) while minimizing I(Xᵢ;Xⱼ) for i≠j — redundancy removal is epistemically correct, not just an efficiency trick.

column1: What is the precise mathematical signature of the curse of dimensionality in a d-dimensional hypercube?
column2: The fraction of volume within distance ε of the boundary is 1 − (1 − 2ε)^d. As d grows (e.g., d=100, ε=0.01 gives ~87%), nearly all data lies near the boundary, and the ratio of max/min pairwise distances approaches 1, degenerating distance-based methods like k-NN.

column1: What is the 'train-serve symmetry' invariant in feature engineering systems?
column2: Every transformation φ applied at training time must be applied identically at serving time, preventing train-serve skew where the model sees differently computed features in production than during training.

column1: How does ML model reproducibility differ fundamentally from Git/source-code reproducibility?
column2: Git reproducibility guarantees bitwise identical outputs; ML reproducibility is statistical — identical inputs can yield slightly different weights due to hardware-level non-determinism (e.g., GPU atomic addition order), so the system must bound and explain variance rather than eliminate it.

column1: Why must published (non-draft) model versions be immutable, and how is this enforced?
column2: Downstream systems reference model versions by hash; mutating artifacts in-place would silently break those references. Immutability is enforced via content-addressable storage, where any modification produces a new hash (i.e., a new version).

column1: Distinguish Covariate Shift, Label Shift, and Concept Drift in terms of which distribution changes.
column2: Covariate Shift: P(X) changes, P(Y|X) stable. Label Shift: P(Y) changes, P(X|Y) stable. Concept Drift: P(Y|X) itself changes — the true input-output relationship has changed, making old data unhelpful.

column1: What is the most operationally common but frequently misdiagnosed form of distributional shift?
column2: Data Quality Drift — schema changes, upstream pipeline bugs, or feature engineering code changes that alter feature statistics without any real-world causal shift; it is often mistaken for concept drift.

column1: State the formal lower bound on production model error under distributional shift.
column2: Error(t) ≥ Error_Bayes + d_H(D_train, D_t), where d_H is the H-divergence between the training distribution and the production distribution at time t.
